canonical_topic: Storage geology: porosity, permeability, and impermeable seals
definition: A storage facility is a porous, permeable underground rock volume where gas dissolves, sealed by a surrounding layer of impermeable rock that keeps it from escaping.
core_idea: Porosity describes how much empty space (pores) a rock contains, while permeability describes whether those pores are interconnected; larger, better-connected pores let gas move in and out faster, and an impermeable cap rock — especially directly above the storage zone, since gas rises — is essential to contain it.
key_points: Storage facilities are geologically similar to natural gas wells and other pressurized containers.
Reusing existing porous rock formations is both structurally sound and far cheaper than excavation, so finding a suitable existing reservoir is one of the biggest tasks in building a new facility.
Porosity = amount of pore space in a rock; permeability = whether pores are connected, allowing flow.
Larger and more interconnected pores increase the speed at which gas can enter or leave the facility.
The impermeable rock layer directly above the storage zone is especially critical because gas naturally rises.
relationships: Underlies why salt caverns (low permeability walls) leak far less than reservoirs or aquifers.
Connects to physically unrecoverable gas — gas embeds in pore walls even in a well-sealed facility.
trading_implications: Geological quality (porosity/permeability/seal integrity) determines a facility's real-world deliverability, not just its stated capacity.
caveats: Confusing porosity (space present) with permeability (whether that space is connected enough to allow flow) — a rock can be porous but not permeable.
